question.knowledge_point: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating
question.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{y}^{3}=4x$ that satisfies $y(0)=1.$  Assume that $y>0.$
question.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x{y}^{3} & =4x \\ 3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x(2+{y}^{3}) \\ \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral on the left-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution

$$
u=2+{y}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Then  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{y}^{2}}{2+{y}^{3}}\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{2+{y}^{3}}(3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+{C}_{2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})+{C}_{2} & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3}) & ={x}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+{y}^{3})} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}} \\ 2+{y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{3} & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}}-2,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}-{C}_{2}}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(0)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{1}^{3} & =K{e}^{{0}^{2}}-2 \\ 1 & =K-2 \\ K & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{y}^{3}=3{e}^{{x}^{2}}-2.
$$

judgment.reasoning: All 16 final answers agree with the supplied worked solutions, but some source explanations contain mathematical errors. q-81506: integrating velocity gives displacement 1/2, hence position 3+1/2=7/2; the first computation line incorrectly uses 7/2 as the initial position. q-120998: displacement is (e^5-e^2)/2, giving (e^2+e^5)/2. q-81509: the triangle has area 3 and the rectangle area 6, so position is -2+9=7. q-18227 and q-73443: the depicted slopes are respectively negative on (0,2) and positive on (0,3). Their source statements that strict monotonicity implies a strictly signed derivative are false in general: a strictly monotone differentiable function can have zero derivative at isolated points. q-132666: the derivative has the sign of 4x-6, hence is negative for x<3/2. q-132667: 4x/(2x^2+1) is negative for x<0. q-48860: ln(x)+1>0 precisely when x>1/e; select the full increasing interval. q-49006: the three marked slopes are negative, positive, and zero at -2, -1, and 1 respectively. q-114698: the half-angle identity gives the antiderivative (sin(x)+x)/2+C. q-31402: substituting u=log_5(3x) gives 2 ln(5) ln|u|+C. q-73655: u=log_4(x) has bounds 1 and 2, yielding 2 ln(4) ln(2)=4(ln(2))^2; the source's first equality incorrectly changes the original x bounds from 4,16 to 2,4. q-79425: setting z=y^3 gives z'=2x(z+2), so z+2=3e^(x^2) after applying y(0)=1. The source incorrectly writes K=±e^(C1-C2): the preceding exponentiation and y>0 require K>0. q-31412: differentiating -5^(-x)/ln(5) gives 5^(-x). q-141738: only II bends upward. q-141740: I and III bend upward. These source errors do not change the selected final answers; every ma_evidence entry quotes only its owning question's supplied solution.
